What makes the chestnut tree so fascinating?

The chestnut tree, which cradles sweet nuts inside a spiky burr, is a signature tree of autumn. A treasure is hidden inside those prickly spines.

content.alt: Chestnut tree - Nature and science facts about the chestnut tree
content.text:
Nature and science facts about the chestnut tree

In June and July, the chestnut tree draws in insects with long white male flowers and their unusual scent, achieving cross-pollination. Come autumn, the burr surrounded by sharp spines fully ripens and splits open into four parts to release the nuts (usually 1 to 3). The thin inner skin of the nut, the pellicle, is rich in tannins, which fend off pests and are also used for dyeing, and the hard timber resists rot, so it's used for posts and furniture.

Great things to observe together

Point out details like the burr (spines that split into four), the nut (outer shell and inner skin), the white male flowers, and the hard timber. It's a great idea to talk together about, "Why does the burr have spines?"

Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on activities

In autumn, examine a burr (carefully!), then peel the nut's outer shell and its bitter inner skin (the pellicle) and compare the two. It's a good idea to talk about the role of the burr's spines (protection).

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why does the chestnut burr have spines?
A. To protect the nuts from animals and pests before they ripen. Once fully ripe, the burr splits open and releases the nuts.

Q. What is the bitter inner skin of the nut?
A. It's called the "pellicle." It's rich in tannins, which fend off pests, and it's also used as a natural dye.

Q. How can we observe this at home?
A. Try examining a burr carefully, peeling and comparing the outer shell and pellicle, and talking about the protective role of the spines.
